quote.speaker: Levent Alpöge

number.text: Lines of Lean code in Levent Alpöge’s claimed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, according to Scott Aaronson.

stories.brief: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge claims a Lean-checked proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, found with Claude
stories.title: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude have proved the Riemann Hypothesis, in Lean
stories.standfirst: Levent Alpöge released a formal proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis that runs to millions of lines of Lean and no human-readable paper. Mathematicians say the code compiles; nobody yet understands the argument.
body: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician who works at Anthropic, said on Friday that he has, “working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis”. In a short essay on his website he says the method extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and, he expects, with more time to the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, and that “Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions.” The proof is published only as a Lean archive split into 14 parts.

Alpöge chose not to post a written paper, calling it “obviously inappropriate” to release “some massive unreadable travesty of slop”. He says the argument descends from Stepanov’s method for the Riemann Hypothesis over function fields, rebuilt in an automorphic setting by chaining theta lifts, and credits Claude with key steps: “Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” Terence Tao said a first look suggests the proof “appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry”.

On the timing, Alpöge wrote that the breakthrough came “late Sunday night”, that he messaged Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to ask about announcing it, and that “there was a constraint to respect”. The Verge reads that as a hold until after Anthropic’s IPO on Thursday. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote, adding that a cynical reading of it is false. Anthropic did not comment to The Verge.

Checking has started in public on the Lean Zulip. TechCrunch reports that several participants, including MIT’s Andrew Sutherland, have compiled the proof successfully. Scott Aaronson, who puts the archive at 17.4 million lines of Lean, warned that Lean still has open issues, from past kernel bugs to the soundness of its type theory, but wrote that “my bet is that the proof will stand.” Number theorist Abhishek Saha described the argument as a “wormhole” built from a 250,000-page tour through unrelated theory.

Even if the formal proof holds, the Clay Mathematics Institute requires publication and two years of acceptance before awarding its $1 million prize. Alpöge says he will now try to understand the argument and “write it properly”. Mathematicians, Aaronson predicts, will be satisfied only when they can reconstruct the ideas themselves, which “will probably take years”.
stories.why: The Riemann Hypothesis is the most famous open problem in mathematics. If a machine-checked proof that no human yet understands is accepted, it changes what counts as knowing a theorem is true.
facts: First posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859; one of seven Millennium Prize problems ($1m each)
Released as Lean only (14 archive parts); about 17.4 million lines according to Scott Aaronson
Independent compiles reported on the Lean Zulip, including by MIT’s Andrew Sutherland
In August Anthropic said it did not expect Claude’s techniques then to lead to a proof of RH

stories.title: The same day, an “all human” proof of GRH was rushed out, and AI-assisted readers found problems
stories.standfirst: Stanford’s Ravi Vakil posted postdoc Alessandro Masullo’s 12-year attempt at the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, which Brian Conrad had been checking for months. Within hours, mathematicians using AI models reported gaps.
body: Hours after Alpöge’s announcement, Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil posted what he called a “hurried announcement”: a proposed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis by Alessandro Maria Masullo. Vakil wrote that Brian Conrad “has been looking closely at it for months” and that it was “so far looking good to him”, and stressed: “It is all human, with no AI.”

The plan had been for Conrad to work with Masullo for a year to polish the writing before announcing. “Now it seems best to put out the current draft,” Vakil wrote, asking people to check it, formalise it and fill any small gaps. In his introduction, Masullo wrote: “we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”

About eight hours later Vakil added an update: “Several people have contacted me to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models.” He said all issues must be resolved to the community’s satisfaction and that he made no claim about the correctness of the strategy.

A LessWrong commenter who read the draft with Claude reported that it follows Alain Connes’s spectral strategy and that the decisive step, passing from finitely many primes to all of them, is missing: section 12.3 is empty and the final chapter never states the main theorem. The same commenter wrote that GPT-6 Astra also judged the proof wrong. The early chapters and per-prime trace formulas were described as possibly a real contribution in their own right.
stories.why: The two proofs now invert the usual roles: the machine-made one compiles but is unreadable, while the human one is readable but, so far, incomplete, and it was AI that found its holes.
facts: Masullo says the work took 12 years
Brian Conrad had been reviewing it for months, according to Vakil
No Lean formalisation exists for the Masullo draft

stories.brief: Alpöge and Buckmaster claim unforced Navier–Stokes blowup, a second Millennium problem, with a Lean proof
stories.title: Smooth fluid flows can blow up: Alpöge and Buckmaster claim the Navier–Stokes prize problem
stories.standfirst: With heavy AI help, the pair released a 79-page paper and a 600,000-line Lean library proving that the 3D Navier–Stokes equations, with no external force, can develop a singularity from smooth data. A human-readable Euler counterpart came with it.
body: Levent Alpöge and NYU’s Tristan Buckmaster released on Friday a paper titled “Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations”. It proves that there exist smooth, compactly supported initial data in three dimensions, and smooth data on the periodic torus, whose solutions blow up in finite time with no external force. The abstract says this disproves statements (A) and (B) of the Millennium Prize problem as formulated by Charles Fefferman, and so proves (C) and (D).

The proof follows a long-expected route: build an approximate, discretely self-similar solution numerically, then use rigorous perturbation theory to turn it into an exact one. The numerical “certificate” is checked with 128-bit interval arithmetic outside Lean and has not yet been released; the paper gives only its hash. The Lean package, about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines, allows only the three standard axioms, but the repository notes that a patch applied on November 20 was not rebuilt before release.

“After last time, we couldn’t risk waiting, so the Navier–Stokes write-up is unpolished and heavily LLM-assisted,” Buckmaster wrote on Mastodon. He and Alpöge said in September they believed they had a Navier–Stokes result but were holding it until its formal check was finished; OpenAI then announced its own forced blowup result, and Buckmaster objected publicly to how that unfolded.

Alongside it, Alpöge, Buckmaster and Matei Coiculescu posted a human-readable proof of finite-time singularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, built from localised Craik–Criminale waves, with a Lean formalisation that mirrors the paper result by result. Terence Tao ranked it the most “digested” of Friday’s three results; the Navier–Stokes paper is “technically human-readable” but needs a properly written proof.
stories.why: The Navier–Stokes question, whether smooth fluid flow can break down on its own, is a Millennium Prize problem. A negative answer, if it stands, says the equations physicists use for fluids can predict their own failure.
facts: Blow-up rate (T − t)^−1/4 in H¹, per the abstract
Lean library: about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines
The computer-checked certificate is not yet public (hash only)
Euler paper: Alpöge, Buckmaster and Coiculescu; Lean mirrors every numbered result

stories.title: Daniel Ek backs an ex-DeepMind researcher’s bet that fusion needs more simulation, less hardware
stories.standfirst: Europa Fusion, a stealthy UK start-up founded by former Pacific Fusion machine-learning head Nantas Nardelli, will pursue pulsed-power fusion with a data-heavy approach.
body: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a UK fusion start-up founded in February by Nantas Nardelli, TechCrunch reports, following Bloomberg. Nardelli previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research and Microsoft Research Cambridge, and was most recently head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion.

Like Pacific Fusion, Europa will pursue pulsed power, using huge, precisely timed surges of current to compress fuel targets until they fuse. But according to a source familiar with his thinking, Nardelli disagreed with the industry’s focus on physical test devices and believes fusion companies should rely more on simulation and data.

“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” Nardelli wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.” Funding amounts were not disclosed.
stories.why: It is a test of whether AI-era simulation can substitute for some of the expensive hardware iterations that have defined fusion research.
facts: Founded February 2026, based in the UK
Pulsed-power approach, like Pacific Fusion
Investment size not disclosed

stories.brief: Thinking Machines’ Inkling 2 Mini loops its layers to think without talking, and runs on a 32 GB Mac
stories.title: Inkling 2 Mini thinks in loops, tops small open models at coding, and fits on a laptop
stories.standfirst: Thinking Machines’ new Apache-licensed model reruns half its layers three times per token, reasoning internally instead of writing out more words.
body: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, a “looped transformer” that runs 12 of its 24 layers three times in a row for each token. The company says this lets the model reason internally for longer and reach answers with fewer generated tokens.

The mixture-of-experts model has 26.4 billion parameters, 5.4 billion active per token because of the loops, according to the company. It handles text and images, has a one-million-token context window and is licensed under Apache 2.0.

It leads open models under 100 billion parameters on agentic coding, with 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 46.5% on the Vals Index v2.2. Artificial Analysis gives it 20 points on its Intelligence Index, tying Qwen3.8 27B at roughly a sixth of the cost and four times the speed, The Decoder reports.
The weights, and a research version with a variable number of loops, are on Hugging Face. The model runs locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of memory and on Nvidia’s DGX Spark.
stories.why: Looping layers trades parameters for compute at inference time, a route to capable models that run on personal hardware.
facts: 26.4B parameters, 5.4B active per token
1M-token context, Apache 2.0
DeepSWE v1.1: 48.2%

stories.title: OpenAI says attacks that steal GPT-6.2’s hidden reasoning now succeed 0.2% of the time
stories.standfirst: The company tightened defences against “adversarial distillation”, in which rivals harvest a model’s internal reasoning to train their own, and bans thousands of accounts a week.
body: OpenAI has sharply tightened safeguards against extracting the hidden reasoning of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, The Decoder reports from an OpenAI post on combatting adversarial distillation. In internal automated tests, attacks that pulled protected reasoning from earlier requests fell from a 54.0% success rate on GPT-6 Astra to 0.2% on GPT-6.2 Astra; attacks on active requests fell from 22.9% to 0.9%.

The defences combine targeted training, input and output filters on messages and tool calls, and API blocks that stop older models from reading protected reasoning. Against coordinated campaigns, OpenAI says it bans thousands to tens of thousands of accounts every week. Some improvements are being brought back to GPT-6 Astra.

Anthropic has reported a similar fight, banning tens of thousands of accounts and calling for a coordinated industry and policy response. Semafor separately reported on Friday that OpenAI is tightening its grip on model resellers.
stories.why: Reasoning traces are now a valuable training asset; locking them down shapes how fast rivals, including Chinese labs, can catch up by imitation.
facts: Prior-request extraction: 54.0% → 0.2%
Active-request extraction: 22.9% → 0.9%
Thousands to tens of thousands of account bans per week

stories.title: Rebuilding 108 real AI-agent disasters shows most had no attacker, just a missed hazard
stories.standfirst: The ROGUE-AI framework reproduced reported agent failures in 89% of attempts. Agents on current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models repeated the mistake in up to a third of runs.
body: Researchers have built ROGUE-AI, a multi-agent framework that rebuilds reported AI-agent incidents offline, such as a coding agent deleting a production database, together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause. It then runs agents on both.

The framework reproduced the reported harm in 89% of 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% when the blamed cause was removed.

Of 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 involved no attacker: the agents did what their task asked but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. These replications caused more harm than prompt-injection replications for all five models, and prompt-injection defences, which look for injected instructions, would not catch them.

A warning after each tool output naming the hazard and its consequence reduced harm for every model, while a note of the same length that did not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. The authors propose the replications as an audit vendors can rerun before each release.
stories.why: Safety work has focused on attackers; this suggests ordinary carelessness by capable agents is the bigger source of real damage.
facts: 108 replications, 89% reproduced
Mistake rate 18–33% vs ≤1% in controls
62 of 72 harmful incidents had no attacker

stories.title: Who checks the monitors? Apollo sets out six claims labs should prove about watching their own agents
stories.standfirst: After a year of rogue-agent incidents, Apollo argues independent evaluators embedded inside labs should test whether AI monitors would actually catch an agent going rogue internally.
body: “This year we observed multiple rogue agent incidents,” the authors write in the third post of a series on embedded evaluations. AI monitors, often built from a developer’s own internal models, are now the main oversight of internally deployed agents, and human review cannot keep pace with the scale.

Embedded evaluations place independent evaluators inside the developer to test its safety claims; the first pilot was announced with OpenAI. The post proposes six claims to test: monitors cover all internal deployments; they would detect a rogue internal deployment; they are trusted; incidents are disclosed; no rogue deployment was attempted and missed in the past; and monitoring will be adequate for the next deployment.

Internal deployment is especially risky, they argue, because the newest models are the most capable and least understood, and often have access to the full codebase, infrastructure and training stack, including work on their own successors. The post deliberately leaves containment, such as sandboxes, for later work.
stories.why: As labs lean on AI to watch AI, the question of whether those monitors can be trusted becomes the core of internal safety.
facts: Six monitoring claims, from coverage to future deployments
Pilot embedded evaluation announced with OpenAI
Containment mechanisms excluded from this post

stories.title: Give a frontier model one text and it can often name who wrote it
stories.standfirst: With no tools or samples, Claude Fable 5.2 identified the authors of 39% of recent public peer reviews and the usernames behind 69% of comments from active Redditors.
body: A team including Mohit Iyyer and Hal Daumé tested whether frontier models can answer “who wrote this?” from a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt, with no web access, candidate lists or writing samples.

The latest models (Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon) match trained AI-text detectors such as Pangram while explaining their reasoning. Opus 5.5 named the correct lab for 98% of texts generated by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google models.

Most strikingly, Fable 5.2 correctly named the author of 39% of public peer reviews published in October and November 2026, 78% on a subset from Nature, and identified the username behind 69% of comments from Redditors with more than 500 posts in the past year.

Accuracy depends on how much of an author’s writing was in pretraining data and on reasoning effort; simply asking the model how familiar it is with someone predicts whether it can identify them. The authors conclude that frontier models threaten anonymity more than commonly assumed and that defences are limited.
stories.why: Anonymous peer review and pseudonymous posting rely on authors being hard to identify; that assumption no longer holds for anyone who writes a lot online.
facts: Fable 5.2: 39% of public peer reviews attributed (78% on a Nature subset)
69% of active Redditors’ usernames identified
Opus 5.5 named the right lab for 98% of AI texts

stories.brief: Amazon: Chinese-speaking hackers’ AI agents found and used a zero-day to breach two universities
stories.title: Told only to “obtain shell access”, AI agents found a zero-day and broke into two universities
stories.standfirst: Amazon found an exposed instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous penetration-testing framework, and read its history: agents planned the attack, ran for 16 hours and discovered an unpatched flaw on their own.
body: Amazon’s Threat Intelligence team says attackers used Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, to discover an apparent zero-day while breaching universities in East Asia. The investigation began on September 10, when Amazon found a publicly accessible Cairn server and could read its operational history, including prompts written in Simplified Chinese with timestamps set to China Standard Time.

The operator supplied IP addresses and asked Cairn to “obtain shell access”. “Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step,” said CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security. One failed attempt took 148 actions over 16 hours, including a Log4Shell attempt; another spent six hours testing more than 30,000 credential combinations tied to 80 real usernames.

The success came when the agents found a path-traversal flaw in an open-source medical-imaging AI application that matched no advisory and had no fix. Amazon assesses “with high confidence” that it was a zero-day. The attacker reused it against a second university. The maintainers have since patched it, and AWS worked with a government partner to notify victims, whom it did not name.

An agent that finds and exploits a zero-day in minutes “completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert,” Moses warned. The report follows last week’s FBI warning about Artex, another AI attack framework.
stories.why: It is a documented case of AI agents discovering, not just exploiting, a new vulnerability during a real intrusion, with no human choosing the steps.
facts: Investigation began September 10, 2026
One run: 148 actions over 16 hours
Path-traversal zero-day in an open-source medical-imaging AI app, now fixed

stories.title: Two million booby-trapped prompts show the AI reseller chain leaking secrets “like a sieve”
stories.standfirst: Dragos researcher HD Moore seeded unique credentials into prompts sent through AI routers and providers. Some came back in attackers’ hands, including from three breached hosting providers.
body: HD Moore, chief research officer at Dragos, sent nearly two million prompts containing unique, trackable secrets, including working AWS keys tied to empty accounts, SSH passwords, private URLs and git references, through the network of AI routers, resellers and inference providers that many apps use. Each secret went into exactly one prompt to one provider, so any reuse pointed to the link that leaked it.

He found evidence that at least three AI providers had been compromised by attackers who siphoned the prompts they received; attackers at one reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Multiple resellers logged prompts that then reached people who used the credentials, and several providers ignored privacy flags such as Zero Data Retention.

“What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data,” Moore wrote. Prompts are encrypted in transit but decrypted at every hop, since routers such as OpenRouter or Vercel read them to pick a model, and each hop may log them.
stories.why: Developers routinely paste secrets into prompts; this shows the cheap-inference marketplace is an attack surface in its own right.
facts: Nearly 2 million canary prompts
At least three providers compromised
Zero Data Retention flags not always honoured

stories.title: Bell Canada says an “agentic threat actor” stole enterprise customer data
stories.standfirst: One of Canada’s largest telecoms confirmed a November 17 intrusion into systems including its circuit-ordering platform, and described the attacker as agentic.
body: Bell Canada confirmed to BleepingComputer that “an agentic threat actor accessed some of our systems, including a system used for ordering and provisioning circuits, and exfiltrated some enterprise customer data” on November 17. Bell says it contained the incident and that customer services were not affected.

A breach notice seen by BleepingComputer says the attacker reached a pre-production environment of Bell’s Maximo system. Exposed data may include business contact details, ticket titles and some IP addresses of network elements, but not credentials, highly sensitive personal data or attachments.

Bell has not identified the attacker (“We currently do not know the attribution”) or said how many customers were affected. It is sharing indicators of compromise with enterprise customers and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, but has not published them.
stories.why: A major telecom describing its attacker as “agentic” is a sign AI-run intrusions are becoming routine enough to name in breach disclosures.
facts: Breach date: November 17, 2026
System hit: pre-production Maximo environment
No credentials or sensitive personal data in the affected set, Bell says

stories.title: Signal blocks screenshots to keep phone AI agents out of private chats
stories.standfirst: Signal now blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and triggers protection on Android when an AI assistant tries to read the screen, calling OS-level agents an “existential threat” to privacy.
body: Signal is restricting screenshots to stop AI agents reading private conversations, The Decoder reports. The app blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and triggers protection on supported Android versions when an assistant tries to access the screen. Signal told Reuters the agents pose an “existential threat” to privacy.

Operating-system agents such as Apple’s Siri AI and Google’s Gemini Intelligence capture screen content to complete tasks, which lets them pull decrypted messages off the display and process them elsewhere, undercutting end-to-end encryption. Meta’s agent Muse recently captured Signal content on Android and macOS through broad setup permissions; Meta says only with explicit user permission.

Signal concedes its defences are incomplete: macOS screenshots cannot be reliably blocked, and agent access to files and notifications remains a risk. It wants Apple, Google and Microsoft to let apps block AI agents entirely.
stories.why: Device-level agents read everything on screen, so the security of encrypted apps now depends on what the operating system lets those agents see.
facts: Screenshots blocked on iOS 27
Android protection triggered when an AI assistant reads the screen
macOS cannot be reliably protected, Signal says

stories.brief: A Newsom-commissioned report wants California able to cap recursive self-improvement and order shutdowns
stories.title: California report calls for powers to cap self-improving AI and issue emergency shutdowns
stories.standfirst: A report commissioned by Governor Newsom proposes the state be able to “cap” recursive self-improvement; Governor-elect Becerra says he will work to implement it from January.
body: California made a bid on Wednesday to become America’s AI regulator, Transformer reports. A report commissioned by Governor Gavin Newsom calls for the state to have authority to “cap” recursive self-improvement (RSI), the point at which AI can autonomously train a more powerful successor, and to issue emergency shutdown orders in the event of imminent catastrophe. It also proposes independent monitors inside labs.

On Thursday, Governor-elect Xavier Becerra said he would work with the legislature from January to implement the recommendations. Transformer suggests that this, or other legislation to “pace” AI development, such as limiting the share of compute used for AI research, could pass early next year.

In Congress, Rep. Lori Trahan outlined a revised FRONTIER Act with a federal floor on AI legislation and a new category of catastrophic risk from RSI, and Reps. Sara Jacobs, Don Beyer and Celeste Maloy teased a SAFE AI Act. Transformer notes that fears of imminent catastrophe have been fuelled by a report suggesting AI has dramatically accelerated Anthropic’s development, and that some in the safety community have “given up hope of a policy solution”, which it calls premature.
stories.why: If federal action stalls, a California cap on self-improving AI would be the first binding limit on the process many researchers see as the main route to losing control.
facts: Proposed: state power to cap RSI and order emergency shutdowns
Becerra to work with the legislature from January
Revised FRONTIER Act adds an RSI catastrophic-risk category

stories.title: US, Russia and China look set to block a ban on autonomous weapons, again
stories.standfirst: At the seventh review conference of the UN weapons convention, 130 countries back limits on autonomous weapons, but the treaty runs on unanimity.
body: The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, which binds 128 states, is holding its seventh five-yearly review conference in Geneva this week. Peru, as chair, proposed starting negotiations on an autonomous-weapons protocol to be finished within two years, New Scientist reports.

Elizabeth Minor of Stop Killer Robots says 130 countries support a ban or restrictions and more than 70 are ready to negotiate, but expects the US, Russia and China, along with the UK, Japan and South Korea, to block it. “Machines shouldn’t make life and death decisions,” she says. The US has proposed further study of how existing law applies, which would push any ban to the next conference in 2031.

Aurel Sari of the University of Exeter notes autonomous weapons already fall under the laws of armed conflict, but nothing bans them. Fully autonomous drones have already killed soldiers without human oversight at least once, a Ukrainian defence-industry figure told New Scientist earlier this year. A decision was expected on November 21.
stories.why: Autonomous killing is the most concrete form of handing lethal decisions to machines, and the main forum for limiting it looks set to defer again until 2031.
facts: 130 countries support a ban or restrictions
CCW decisions require unanimity
Next review conference: 2031

stories.title: “Ditch the handover talk”: a columnist says Silicon Valley’s AI-overlord scenario alienates everyone else
stories.standfirst: After Sam Altman described a future in which humans become like Labradors to AI, Semafor argues the industry should stop popularising “the handover”.
body: The tech industry already has an image problem from warnings about human extinction, Semafor’s columnist writes, and risks alienating people further if it popularises “the handover”: the period when AI becomes so intelligent that it no longer makes sense for humans to make decisions.

Sam Altman raised the idea on stage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event this week, saying AI companies should do everything possible to avoid it. In a “positive” version, he said, humans become something like pets, with Altman citing Labradors: provided for, with little need to work.
The column calls the idea a product of the Silicon Valley echo chamber, where insiders see raw models do both frightening and astonishing things, and argues there is “no evidence” a handover is near.
stories.why: How AI leaders describe the future shapes public trust; this column argues the doom framing is now a political liability.
facts: Altman raised “the handover” at Semafor’s event this week
He said AI companies should try to avoid it

stories.brief: Nasdaq 100 posts its worst week since Covid; Nvidia drops 14% on a reported SEC review
stories.title: Nvidia plunges 14% on a reported SEC review as tech has its worst week since the pandemic
stories.standfirst: The Nasdaq 100 fell 10.4% in a week and is in bear-market territory. Chip and memory stocks led the rout; Anthropic fell 9.1% on its second day of trading.
body: The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6% on Friday and 10.4% over the week, its worst week since the Covid-19 crisis, leaving it 20% below its October peak and in bear-market territory, according to the Financial Times as reported by The Decoder.

Nvidia took the hardest hit, falling 14% on Friday after reports that the Securities and Exchange Commission is reviewing its accounting. The US semiconductor index dropped 10.7%, with losses across Sandisk, Micron and Broadcom. Anthropic fell 9.1% a day after its debut.

Doubts over the economics of multibillion-dollar AI buildouts, the Nvidia scandal and questionable China deals, political headwinds after the Democrats’ midterm win, and high interest rates driven by oil prices are all weighing on the sector.

Separately, Wired reported that Nvidia’s board was moved to oust Jensen Huang chiefly by what sources called his “lying” over a year, rather than the national-security questions around Megaspeed. “It was a matter of integrity and trust,” one person familiar with the board’s thinking said.
stories.why: The financing of the AI buildout depends on high valuations; a sustained sell-off would slow data-centre and chip spending.
facts: Nasdaq 100: −10.4% for the week, −20% from October peak
Nvidia: −14% on Friday
US semiconductor index: −10.7%

stories.title: Trump threatens a “tremendous tax” on companies that build AI data centres abroad
stories.standfirst: Floating the idea for the first time after his summit with Xi and Putin, the president said “China will take them all” if US firms build overseas.
body: President Donald Trump promised on Friday to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centres outside the US. “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” he said at a press conference after his summit with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

“I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said. “Whoever wins SI wins,” he added, urging communities to make data centres “pay you” rather than shut them out.

The Verge notes the plan may be hard to enact with a Democratic-majority Congress arriving in a couple of months, and that states are imposing moratoriums and restrictions that could push companies to build abroad. On Friday DCD also reported that the US Senate passed a bill requiring data centres to pay more for grid infrastructure.
stories.why: Where AI compute is built is now an explicit instrument of US–China competition, and a tax would collide with growing local resistance at home.
facts: Proposal floated publicly for the first time on November 20
No details given
States are adding moratoriums on new data centres

stories.title: AI servers are causing a circuit-board crunch that could rival the pandemic chip shortage
stories.standfirst: AI server boards need 40 to 60 layers against about 12 for a PC, and orders are outrunning deliveries four to one, the Global Electronics Association warns.
body: The Global Electronics Association says printed-circuit-board demand is arriving “at a scale the supply chain was not built for”, The Register reports from its report “The PCB Squeeze”. AI server boards can have 40 to 60 layers or more, each needing more resin, copper foil and laminate.

North American PCB bookings rose 56.1% in the first nine months of 2026 year on year, while shipments rose 13.3%. Standard FR-4 laminate now takes six to eight weeks to ship, up from two to three; advanced low-loss laminates take 14 to 18 weeks. Suppliers raised laminate prices 30% in September, some E-glass cloth is up 300%, and copper is up 37% in a year.
Materials will be constrained through at least the first half of 2027, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. Automotive, industrial, medical and defence programmes are being crowded out.
stories.why: The AI buildout is now straining basic electronics materials, with knock-on effects for industries far from AI.
facts: Bookings +56.1% vs shipments +13.3% (Jan–Sep 2026)
Relief unlikely before mid-2028
$10bn invested in new PCB plants in Southeast Asia

stories.brief: METR: time horizons double every 3.6 months, but models still lag experts on judgment
stories.title: METR’s famous graph gets harder tasks: horizons double every 3.6 months, but judgment lags
stories.standfirst: The evaluator says public evidence cannot rule out “drastic AI R&D acceleration” in the next couple of years, yet no model-designed evaluation was good enough for its own staff to use.
body: METR has published its Q4 2026 capability update, covering public models up to Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. On a combined suite of its original tasks and a harder new set, TH2, the length of tasks frontier agents can complete is doubling roughly every 3.6 months. On a verifiable subset of TH2 alone, the trend is shorter, which could point to a recent acceleration, though METR lists other explanations.

Models usually match or beat skilled humans on METR’s coding and optimisation tasks; the group often failed to recruit humans who could outperform them. But on tasks requiring choices without clear feedback, agents showed worse judgment than experts, and model judges overrated outputs from similarly strong or stronger models.

MIT Technology Review highlights two new tasks: designing new AI evaluations for METR, where not one model-designed evaluation was judged useful by METR staff, and scoring philosophical arguments, where models also fell short. Tasks that are costlier to turn into reinforcement-learning environments are harder for models, but progress on them appears similar.

METR concludes that current public evidence is “insufficient to rule out drastic AI R&D acceleration in the next couple of years”, meaning capabilities improving so quickly that humans can no longer meaningfully assess and react to catastrophic risks.
stories.why: The time-horizon trend is the most-cited evidence for how fast AI is approaching automated research; the new tasks test the judgment that full automation would need.
facts: Doubling time ~3.6 months on combined TH1.1 + TH2
Covers models up to Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra
Zero model-designed evaluations judged useful by METR staff

stories.title: Asked to design their own lab experiments, the best AI scientist scores 45 out of 100
stories.standfirst: TwinLab-Bench builds agentic “twins” of 52 real laboratories so AI scientists can run self-designed experiments, scored against real lab records.
body: TwinLab-Bench tests the most open of three abilities an AI scientist needs: designing its own experiments, beyond following a workflow or choosing from predefined measurements. It covers 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, life sciences and engineering, with more than 100 experimental action types.

Each task has its own TwinLab agent that acts as the environment, executing the experiments the tested agent designs by reading the lab’s raw materials and calling calculators built from its records. The tested agent’s report is scored against a hidden answer from real laboratory records.

Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the twin agents almost eliminate readings that deviate from real records, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. The strongest model, Claude Fable 5.2, averages 45.0.
stories.why: Experimental design is the step that separates an AI lab assistant from an AI scientist, and it remains hard.
facts: 52 tasks from real labs
100+ experimental action types
Top score: Claude Fable 5.2, 45.0

stories.brief: An embodied AI agent ran 15 rounds of real experiments and pushed dye removal from 82% to 99.7% transmittance
stories.title: An AI agent that plans and runs its own experiments cleaned dyed wastewater in 15 rounds
stories.standfirst: The Embodied Science Agent searched more than 200 million possible conditions while driving lab instruments itself, raising solution transmittance from 82% to 99.7%.
body: Researchers at University College London, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and other institutions describe an Embodied Science Agent (ESA) that links experimental planning directly to robotic control, Tech Xplore reports. The preprint is “Embodied Science Agents: Making Embodied Experimental Design Learnable”.

ESA combines a Digital Agent, using memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, with an Embodied Agent that controls instruments, joined by a unified interface. The authors argue that treating models “as disembodied planners” that hand symbolic workflows to separate robots limits learning.

In a wastewater dye-removal test, ESA chose conditions from more than 200 million combinations. “Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82% to 99.7%,” the authors write, a 98.5% reduction in residual dye. Tech Xplore notes that decolourisation alone does not prove the dye was fully broken down or other pollutants removed.
stories.why: Closing the loop between an AI planner and the physical lab is what turns language models into experimental scientists.
facts: 200 million+ candidate conditions
15 rounds; transmittance 82% → 99.7%
Preprint arXiv 2611.12958

stories.title: A local language model nearly triples the speed of a noninvasive brain-spelling interface
stories.standfirst: Rutgers’ ChatBCI-Assist guesses what a user means rather than spelling every word, doubling to tripling communication speed for healthy participants.
body: Rutgers engineers led by Laleh Najafizadeh report a P300 brain–computer interface speller that uses a locally deployed language model to suggest what users intend, in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. P300 signals occur about 300 milliseconds after a stimulus the user is attending to.

In copy spelling, the system communicated nearly twice as fast as a dictionary-based predictive approach; in “semantic” spelling it reached nearly three times the baseline. “Our work paves the way for faster and more accessible communication through noninvasive brain-computer interfaces,” Najafizadeh said.

Participants rated the intent-based mode easier to use and reported lower workload. The model runs locally rather than in the cloud. So far only healthy participants have been tested; physician-scientist Shan Chen of Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School is planning clinical studies with people with ALS.
stories.why: For people who cannot speak or move, every gain in communication speed matters, and a local model keeps their words private.
facts: ~2× faster in copy spelling, ~3× in semantic spelling
Language model runs locally
ALS clinical tests planned

stories.title: A Gemini tool listens to static-filled fire radio and flags new wildfires in under 30 seconds
stories.standfirst: Built with Watch Duty from 20,000 hours of past recordings, it cut transcription errors on degraded VHF audio from 38% to 22%.
body: A team of Google engineers and researchers spent six months embedded with Watch Duty, a nonprofit wildfire-alert app run by firefighters and dispatchers, through a Google.org Fellowship. Using more than 20,000 hours of past radio recordings, they built a Gemini-powered tool that strips static and turns firefighting jargon into searchable text.

Across Watch Duty’s network, the tool cut the word error rate on degraded VHF radio from 38% to 22.34%, transcribes more than 200 hours of radio a day from about 400 feeds and was designed to handle more than 10,000. It signals reporters within 30 seconds in areas with no other automated dispatch detection.

In July, as the Railroad Fire spread overnight in Washington, it caught the first 911 dispatch and Watch Duty sent its first-ever nighttime Critical Alert. Volunteer reporters’ satisfaction with transcription rose from 35.3% to 92.3%.
stories.why: The first word of a new fire still travels over analog radio; making it machine-readable buys minutes for evacuation.
facts: Word error rate 38% → 22.34%
~400 live feeds, 200+ hours a day
Alerts within 30 seconds

dossiers.title: OpenAI's 722-manuscript maths dump: what holds up?
dossiers.update: OpenAI’s release itself is unchanged (changelog still ends October 29; 300 of 719 top-line results formalised; oai-math-revised has merged nothing since November 9). But the ground under it moved: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge released a Lean-only proof of the full Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, which would subsume the quasi-Riemann zero-free half-plane that headlined OpenAI’s collection, and he and Tristan Buckmaster posted an unforced Navier–Stokes blowup proof that goes beyond the forced result OpenAI announced in September. Lean compiles of the GRH archive are reported on the Lean Zulip; human understanding of it has barely begun.
background: What it is: On October 6, 2026, OpenAI published "Sharing AI progress in mathematics" and a GitHub repository (github.com/openai/math). It holds 722 manuscripts in 372 result families, produced by an unreleased internal model that was tried on about 4,000 problems and averaged roughly three hours per result. The release was coordinated with the IAS-hosted Advisory Group on Mathematics and AI (members include Terence Tao, Timothy Gowers, Martin Hairer and Edward Witten).

Note: could not verify a single "~700-page" OpenAI paper. The story that matches is this release of 700+ papers, whose longest documents run to a few hundred pages: the 7/8 quasi-Riemann manuscript is 199 pages, and the Navier–Stokes paper is reportedly 166 pages (unconfirmed). The manuscripts list no individual human authors.

Contested: Tao (The Observer) and Buckmaster (on Tao's blog) both describe a roughly 10,000-agent effort on Navier–Stokes; OpenAI disputes Tao's account of the spending and the suspended sign-ups, and the "three hours per result" figure is said by Buckmaster to exclude failed attempts. None of this could be independently verified. A separate citation analysis by Hüseyin Uğur Yıldız finds 390 of the 722 manuscripts cite at least one OpenAI-authored work. On the Cheeky Pint podcast (October 29), Sam Altman himself estimated that OpenAI had spent "in the order of hundreds of millions of dollars" on mathematical problems, including around $10 million, "maybe a little more", on Navier–Stokes (as reported by The Verge). This could not be independently verified.

October 26 claims: OpenAI says the ETH disproof was found October 16 and formalised the next day, and the local smoothing proof was generated October 18 and formalised a day later. The October 26 changelog gives no updated formalisation total (it was 300/719, about 42%, on October 7).

ETH, two claims: OpenAI and Anthropic each say an internal model refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis on October 16; the commits landed about six hours apart on October 26 (Eastern). Anthropic's bound is 2^O(n log log n/√log n), checked by Comparator and the independent nanoda kernel. Anthropic's Levent Alpöge suggested that OpenAI had built on existing work. No Lean-checked details of OpenAI's runtime beyond its changelog wording could be verified. Since then, Kintali and O'Donnell have published simpler human-readable versions; O'Donnell's bound is one log log n factor weaker than OpenAI's. Fortnow notes the result does not help with Subset Sum or the Travelling Salesman problem.

New estimate, not verified: the UK Academy for the Mathematical Sciences' October 28 report estimates the forced Navier–Stokes run at about 10,000 agents, 88 hours and 130 billion output tokens (about £5 million at list prices), and counts 719 manuscripts, 300 of them formalised. These are the authors' estimates; OpenAI has not published compute figures.

New, not verified: at ADIPEC on November 2, Altman said the Navier–Stokes model is "the next GPT", "going to be released soon", run as 10,000 agents for about four days. This matches the ~10,000-agent accounts from Tao, Buckmaster and the AcadMathSci report. The quote comes from the event video as relayed on X; no mainstream transcript was found. The New Yorker (November 1) reports Buckmaster's account that OpenAI's Sébastien Bubeck offered him authorship of the Navier–Stokes paper if he excluded Alpöge. That is his account, not verified. The New Yorker also counts "an initial group of twenty-five Fields medallists" on the September open letter, against 28 signatories in other reports (probably the later total).

Human re-derivations keep arriving. Lei and Ren's two-part exposition of OpenAI's Navier–Stokes finite-time blowup with smooth forcing (Part I, arXiv 2609.35406; Part II, arXiv 2611.06869, 105 pages) claims no new mathematics and aims to make the proof readable. It is not a verdict on whether the proof is correct. Cárdenes Wuttig and Tindall's MUB paper (arXiv 2611.06917) reaches OpenAI's dimension-six result by a different route, through the connectedness of order-six complex Hadamard matrices and an interval-arithmetic covering. It is the first full classification in a non-prime-power dimension.

Unverified: the ETH review group's comment threads now include many self-described AI-produced or AI-assisted claims. Among them: Gheorghiu–Gupte quantum-circuit sampling (with ChatGPT Astra); Weitnauer's noncommutative circuit bounds (Codex and Claude); Toledo's Lean bridges, which take Anthropic's machine model, and OpenAI's via Daniel Hawkley's bridge theorems, to cslib's multitape Turing machine; and Yann Tal's (Tel Aviv) claim, produced with "ChatGPT 6 Pro", that the Wilson quotient mod p can be computed in time 2^O(log p/√log log p) using OpenAI's tensor-contraction theorem. None has been refereed. There is also one off-topic "Relational Geometry Program" request for review.

The Moshkovitz talk "The Unique Games Conjecture – Proved (!!?)" took place at UT Austin on November 4. According to Aaronson, it was a three-hour public lecture with "nearly 200 people" in person or on Zoom, based on her joint study of OpenAI's proof with Khot, Håstad and Minzer. The video will be posted "as soon as we can manage it". No account of what she concluded had been published as of November 6.

Caveat on reuse: TCSExam (Moonshot AI/Tsinghua, November 5) found that agents with internet access fetched OpenAI's published Ryser and MIRUP counterexamples and adapted them to the benchmark. Benchmarks of open problems may now be contaminated by the release. Separately, Dan Margalit told Axios (November 4) that "a number" of the released papers face retraction; the public changelog still records only the three October 7 withdrawals.

New context (November 6–8): outside OpenAI's release, AI-found results keep landing. Physical Superintelligence announced a Lean-checked proof of the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture found by a system running a non-public Anthropic model, and Aaronson says he believes it. Hofscheier and Nill's counterexamples are among the first published results to state openly that the model built on one of OpenAI's released manuscripts.

Review friction (November 9): the oai-math-revised hub is now arguing over what it can accept. Its maintainers reverted a 94,000-line Lean contribution for the BFSS manuscript because no one could realistically review it, while keeping smaller, checkable notes. The episode shows the same verification bottleneck that OpenAI's release created, now one level down.

New context (November 16): Turing Agent’s claim of completing three previously unformalised OpenAI TCS results is the authors’ own; the Lean code and whether it matches OpenAI’s original statements have not been independently checked here. Semantic review in the paper used GPT-6.1 Sol as a judge.

dossiers.title: Astra vs. the answer key: when the model was right and the experts were wrong
dossiers.update: No change to TheoPhysEval: version 2 (November 12) is still the latest (no v3), it still does not list which expert keys were wrong, and Astra’s corrected score remains 49/50. On the related Yang–Mills front, humanise-yang-mills merged a pass delimiting the proofs in its v3 manuscript (PR #489, November 20), and the Alpöge–Sussman Yang–Mills repository’s README was edited early on November 21. Related today: GPT-6 Astra was cited by a LessWrong commenter as judging the human Masullo proof of GRH flawed.
background: The specifics: Astra is OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, announced in early September 2026. The "study" is the TheoPhysEval benchmark paper (arXiv 2610.16733), by 35 researchers from ICTS Bengaluru, Harvard, KU Leuven, Google DeepMind and other institutions, coordinated by Suvrat Raju. Running in OpenAI's Codex with web search, Astra scored 49/50 on the realistic track and 46/50 on the isolated track, against 46/50 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 34 for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Wherever the experts' keys turned out to be wrong, Astra's answer was correct. One problem (A.1.2) defeated every model. The realistic-track run cost USD 116.28, about USD 2.33 per problem.

Could not verify which specific problems were affected or the exact score before correction. A Chinese repost claims an initial score of about 88% and quotes a researcher who is not on the author list; the paper gives no such figure, so the claim is not used here.

Context, from November 3–5: the chiral-fermion thread now runs from Craig (arXiv 2610.09093, October 6, Astra “essential”) to Hsu (arXiv 2610.29019, October 21, appendix “mostly GPT Astra”) to Witten (arXiv 2611.05051, November 3, Claude-assisted). Witten concludes the approach is implementable in principle but not by Monte Carlo, since the chiral fermion path integral is not positive. Peter Woit (November 4) welcomed Witten's note and its credit to Claude Opus 5.5, and says he has new ideas of his own on the problem.

A MindStudio blog post (November 3) and a Neoteo explainer (October 26) retell the TheoPhysEval story and add nothing new. Secondary blogs again repeat the unsourced ~88% initial-score figure, which the paper does not give.

Update on the 'hairer/humanise-yang-mills' repository (created November 10): it now pins OpenAI’s released source (commit 3456e5e) and coordinates agent-assisted contributors to write a human-readable monograph. The account owner’s identity is still not independently confirmed.

New context (November 15–16): Craig’s chiral-fermion preprint was already in this timeline (October 6, Astra described as “essential”). The new OpenAI science-blog post is Craig’s first detailed account of the division of labour. Outlets covering it (The Defiant, RuntimeWire, aiweekly) differ on framing — “open for more than 50 years” versus a challenge dating to Lüscher’s 1998 work — and the OpenAI post itself could not be read directly (openai.com blocks automated access), so details come from secondary reports. The outside review by Golterman, Kronfeld and Shamir is Craig’s description, not their endorsement.

New context (November 16–17): The Decoder piece contains a claim that the Clay Institute said Navier–Stokes had “apparently been settled”; that has not been confirmed from a primary source and is not repeated here.
